bed4b88baa6fc062: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — When Violet Lee Zi Yi began researching Malaysian Chinese youths, she admitted she initially approached the community with assumptions about its relative economic advantages, resources and access to opportunities.
What she discovered through interviews with these youths across Peninsular Malaysia was a much more complicated picture.

“I initially thought Chinese is a unitary block. It is so different,” Lee said in an interview about the findings of IMAN Research’s report, Kami Orang Sini Juga: Chinese Youths and Democratic Belonging — The Politics of Pragmatism and Fairness.
The report, prepared by Lee and co-researcher Liew Liang Hong, is based on interviews with 116 Malaysian Chinese youths aged between 18 and 35 conducted from August 2025 to April 2026.
It examines Chinese youths on how they understand their identity, navigate opportunities and inequality, and relate to politics and public institutions.

Rather than treating Malaysian Chinese youths as a single political or cultural group, the research found that their experiences were shaped by factors including family history, language, schooling, religion, socioeconomic background and where they grew up.
For some, regional identities such as being Penangite, Johorean or an anak Terengganu were just as important in defining who they were.
“When I started the research, I went into it with a mindset of — apa lagi Cina mahu or what else do the Chinese want?
“I wanted to understand what more Malaysian Chinese youths wanted, so I had assumptions about the community’s relative advantages.
“But the interviews changed my perception. Everyone’s experience is so diverse, so different, and every conversation just added what I had never imagined before,” she said.
One example was how family history could shape identity differently across generations.

Lee said she had not initially considered how being a third-generation Malaysian Chinese could produce a different outlook from being fourth-generation, depending on how grandparents and great-grandparents had spoken about China and their family’s history.
She said these differences emerged naturally during the conversations, illustrating how the research uncovered experiences that the team had not anticipated when designing its questions.
Belonging is not always straightforward
The report found that national identity did not necessarily come at the expense of Chinese cultural identity.
Some participants described themselves primarily as Malaysian, while others considered Malaysian Chinese an inseparable identity.
Others placed strong emphasis on their state or hometown.
For some interviewees from the East Coast, being an anak Terengganu was central to how they described home, even as they recognised restrictions associated with being part of a minority community.

One participant described the distinction between feeling at home and feeling politically restricted, saying: “As a layman I feel I belong, but in politics I feel being restricted, like in Matriculation and fund allocation.”
The report said these feelings could coexist: participants could feel emotionally attached to Malaysia while questioning how public resources and institutions treated different communities.
It also found that everyday interactions could foster a sense of shared Malaysian identity.
Participants spoke positively about ordinary experiences such as eating at mamak restaurants, mixing languages and joining one another’s festivals.

However, the researchers cautioned against romanticising these interactions, noting that cordial relationships did not necessarily translate into deeper understanding or erase concerns about institutional fairness.
The cost of pragmatism
One of the report’s central findings is what it calls “self-cornering” — the tendency to find private ways around perceived problems rather than challenge the institutions behind them.
The report found that some young people responded to uncertainty over public opportunities by working harder, relying on family networks, paying for alternatives or looking overseas.
These decisions could be practical and help individuals secure their futures, but the researchers argued that they also carried wider consequences.

When those with sufficient resources could find private alternatives, the institutions and policies behind their concerns remained unchanged. Those without the means to find alternatives could be left with fewer options.
The report also distinguished between inequality personally experienced by participants, barriers they anticipated and accounts they had heard from family or community members.
It cautioned against treating every disappointing outcome as proof of discrimination, while recognising that inherited accounts could influence how young people assessed their prospects.
Wanting to be heard
Another finding concerned the distance between young people and the organisations or institutions expected to represent them.
Lee said she was struck by how some interviewees did not consider their own opinions valuable simply because they were not politically vocal.
“We wanted to include young people who were not already active in community organisations or political circles, rather than relying mainly on those who were accustomed to speaking publicly.
“Only about 10 to 15 per cent of those recruited were young leaders.

“This was important because young people who were already involved in organisations were often more comfortable expressing their views, while others might not see their own experiences as worth sharing,” she said.
The research team also found that established community leaders could say they wanted younger people to participate, yet were sometimes reluctant to give them meaningful space.
Lee said this could leave young people struggling to find where they could contribute, while older leaders continued to hold the resources and decision-making positions.

She also questioned the narrow definition of success within parts of the community, where financial achievement and professional status could be valued more visibly than civic or political participation.
“Chinese youth are not rewarded socially if you are in politics. Only if you become a politician, you become someone famous, then yes, you’re recognised,” she said.
Those working behind the scenes, she added, were less likely to receive recognition.
Lee said the research also found that some young people wanted to move beyond racialised political thinking but were unsure how to do so.
“They are conditioned in the racial politics. They are conditioned into thinking along the communal lines, but they want to break through that.”
Among the many challenges
She said one challenge for the researchers was to ensure that the findings did not simply reflect the views of the loudest or most visible members of the community.
“Being the loudest did not mean that they have a full understanding of a stipulation on ground,” she said.
Not particularly looking for a solution, Lee said the report is a qualitative research and is not statistically representative of all Malaysian Chinese youths.
“Its findings are intended to provide insight into how the participants understood their experiences, rather than measure how widespread particular views are.

“We actually only included 30 per cent of the data collected, there were just too much data which we thought was better to leave them for further research into specific communities and experiences,” she said.
For Lee, the next step is to create more opportunities for young people from different communities to speak to one another.
She said the responsibility should not fall on young people alone, but also on researchers, the media and civil society organisations to create space for discussion.
For her, the research is ultimately about giving young people more room to think about their place in the country, rather than seeing them only as voters whose views matter during elections.
“This research gets the conversation starting especially for Chinese youths who don’t know where to start, or what to do first,” she said.

432961bd20a01d3c: Britain’s Royal Navy has formally commissioned its first uncrewed boat squadron, operating seaborne drones on front-line operations as part of its “Hybrid Navy” strategy.

The force says the 1st Autonomous Squadron officially entered active service on November 5 at a ceremony in Portsmouth Naval Base. It comprises around 180 personnel, about the same as a Type 23 frigate, split into two watches to enable operations around the clock.

This active squadron replaces Project Beehive, the navy’s experimental program to build a fleet of autonomous and remotely operated vessels, through which it obtained 20 uncrewed boats from UK-based Kraken Technology Group.
The force is understood to be using both Kraken’s K3 Scout, and the SM400 from SYOS Aerospace, known by the Royal Navy as the Rattler.

The K3 Scout is an 8.4 m boat capable of 55 knots and can carry a payload of up to 600 kg. It has a range of up to 650 nautical miles and endurance of up to 7 days. The maker describes it as capable of a range of missions, including anti-ship and anti-submarine to detecting and countering other drones and even casualty evacuation.

The Rattler boat is 7.2 m and has a 500 kg modular bay, with a range of up to 950 nautical miles. It was used last year in a demonstration during which 5 of the uncrewed boats were remotely-piloted to escort patrol ship HMS Tyne and mine countermeasures mothership HMS Stirling Castle

Part of the new squadron’s mission will be to act as pathfinder for drone operations, working on bringing additional types of uncrewed surface vessel (USVs) into fleet service and conducting a range of operations alongside other organizations – both as single vessels and as part of a task group.

The “Hybrid Navy” concept was outlined by First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins earlier this year, who made the case that uncrewed vessels would be vital in filling the gaps left by the Royal Navy’s much depleted surface fleet.

Speaking at the launch of the autonomous squadron, Fleet Commander Vice-Admiral Steve Moorhouse hailed it as an historic occasion, but warned that the seas are becoming more contested, more dangerous and harder to operate in.
“A hybrid navy is about giving our people better tools. It means more reach, more striking power and more options,” he stated.

Last week, the force also launched strike drones from one of its aircraft carriers for the first time. Nyan one-way drones made by BAE Systems were launched from the deck, as well as a Tekever AR5 fixed-wing uncrewed aircraft, the same kind the British Army has selected to replace its troublesome Watchkeeper fleet.

Elsewhere, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it has launched a British-built satellite called Titania into orbit, claiming it “gives the Armed Forces a new pair of eyes in space.” However, the original purpose of the orbiter was understood to be to test high-speed optical communications from low Earth orbit directly to Earth, using laser beams that are harder to intercept than radio links.

Titania is the second satellite in the UK’s growing constellation of military satellites in orbit, following the launch of Tyche in October, and will be operated by UK Space Command as part of the ISTARI* program.
The latter aims to deliver satellites and supporting ground systems to expand space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, the MoD said.
However, while the satellite is British-made, it got into space via an American rocket, riding on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 mission. ®
* What is it with the tech industry and Tolkien references?

1412273beae0e596: NEW YORK: A top Federal Reserve official said Tuesday that the US central bank must act swiftly and forcefully to address inflation, signalling plans to back an interest rate hike in December.

"Inflation remains too high," Fed governor Christopher Waller said during an address in London. "Monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2% in the medium term."

The speech came a few hours ahead of the release later Tuesday of key US consumer price inflation (CPI) data for October. Waller, in the speech, said he would consider a double-sized 0.5 percentage point increase in interest rates if the October CPI report shows another significant uptick in pricing pressures.

Waller's statement boosts the likelihood that the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next month will lift interest rates for the second time in three meetings, posing another setback for US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pushed for lower rates and whose Republican Party suffered sweeping defeats in last week's midterm elections.
In September, CPI accelerated to 0.6% on a month-on-month basis, while rising 3.7% on a year-on-year basis, due in part to surging gasoline prices related to the US-Iran war.
Waller, who was appointed by Trump in 2020 to the Fed's seven-member Board of Governors, called the September data "bad", with "no silver lining".

Waller cited inflationary effects from the artificial intelligence buildout and pointed to Fed research that suggests "energy price pressures may pass through to goods and services in a more sustained way than in the past."

"Even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting," Waller said.
But if October pricing dynamics are similar to last month's, "then a stronger policy move may be needed," he said.

"In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take."

e7372b2100ebfac3: Microsoft is retiring its free education email service, leaving schools, colleges, and universities facing new licensing bills if they want to keep students' mailboxes.

The company announced plans last week to retire Office 365 A1, the Student Use Benefit program, and free Exchange Online for Alumni. The changes generally take effect at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028.

Office 365 A1 provides eligible institutions with web-based Office applications, Teams, and email at no charge. Its replacement, Microsoft 365 Education A0, excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also depends on paid faculty licensing and students actively using Windows devices for education.

A spokesperson for the UK's Department for Education told The Register: "We are disappointed that Microsoft has made this decision. However, we are pleased to have successfully negotiated some additional concessions for the UK, giving schools, colleges and universities the time they need to be able to successfully transition to new licensing agreements."

An industry insider said the loss of free Microsoft-hosted email could add thousands to institutions' bills. Another organization noted "significant concerns… around affordability, equitable treatment across the sector, and the longer-term implications of the changes."

A spokesperson for UK education technology body Jisc told The Register that its "focus has been on ensuring that UK education providers are well supported and have sufficient time to assess their options."
"We continue working closely with Microsoft and sector partners to support those discussions and help institutions make informed decisions about their future requirements."

Also being retired are free Exchange Online for Alumni – which lets graduates retain their mailboxes – and the Student Use Benefit, providing student licenses at no additional charge when institutions purchase qualifying faculty licenses. Microsoft plans a paid alumni replacement.

The Windows giant is also changing storage entitlements and introducing Microsoft 365 Education A7, its "most advanced education offering," which adds AI, security, governance, and device-management features.
Asked why it was removing those services from the free tier, Microsoft framed the overhaul as a response to institutions' changing needs.

A spokesperson told The Register: "Education institutions are evaluating AI, security, privacy, governance, and teaching and learning as connected priorities rather than separate technology decisions.

"Microsoft is updating the portfolio now to provide a clearer path from foundational access to advanced capabilities, while enabling institutions to adopt technology according to their needs and readiness. This evolution reflects both the value Microsoft 365 Education has gained since the last pricing change nearly a decade ago and the structure of the new portfolio.

"Microsoft's broader goal is not technology adoption for its own sake. It is to support AI and digital experiences that strengthen learning, preserve educator judgment and give institutions the controls they need to manage data, privacy, and responsible use."

Office 365 A1 stopped accepting new web-direct orders on November 5, 2026, with partner-channel sales ending on May 1, 2027. Retirement is scheduled for January 1, 2028, but existing agreements remain valid through their current terms. Institutions that need continued service must move to replacement licenses at the applicable renewal or contract expiry. ®

5c7becfbff02111f: NOVEMBER 10 — When I first read the court order concerning former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak’s release following payment of his RM50 million fine, two thoughts immediately crossed my mind.
My first was that the document was fake. Just look at the heading: Order of discharge on payment of fine.
Then came the second line, which read: In the Tinggi Court of Wilayah Persekutuan.
Where on earth can you find a “Tinggi Court” in Malaysia? Surely, this must be a fake court document.

I shared my observation with a source close to the matter, who insisted that the document was genuine. I remained unconvinced, pointing out further evidence that suggested something was seriously wrong with it.
For one, the document switches between English and Bahasa Melayu, sometimes within the same sentence. Having seen and read court documents before, I found this rather odd and unprofessional.
This brings me to my second observation.

The document appears to have been prepared in a hurry, with typos scattered throughout. Apart from the person who drafted it, I doubt anyone checked or edited its spelling, sentence structure or contents.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Datuk Seri Najib Razak is pictured at the Kuala Lumpur Court Complex, in Kuala Lumpur November 25, 2025. — Picture by Firdaus Latif
Najib’s lawyers, who applied for the order, should have noticed these errors if they bothered to read and check the document. They, too, bear some responsibility for the mistakes and inconsistencies.

Although the document is addressed to the officer-in-charge of Kajang prison, the background information about the prisoner appears to list only one charge under Section 406 of the Penal Code, repeated three times, instead of identifying the three charges under three different Acts.
Even the client’s name is inconsistent, appearing sometimes with “Mohd” and sometimes without it.
But the most puzzling part is the last paragraph in the first column, which reads:

“Sekiranya Dato Seri Najib... tidak mematuhi mana-mana syarat-syarat tersebut, maka Perintah ini adalah terbatal dan Dato Seri Najib... hendaklah secara serta-merta meneruskan baki hukuman di Penjara Kajang atau di mana-mana penjara yang ditetapkan oleh Komisioner Jeneral Penjara. or to Menjalani hukuman baki secara tahanan di rumah yang beralamat di No. 11, Jalan Langgak Duta, Taman Duta...”
The mixing of Bahasa Melayu and English in this paragraph is not only poor but also confusing. A sentence cannot simply begin with the lowercase English word “or” and continue in Bahasa Melayu.
More importantly, how is anyone supposed to interpret a sentence that appears to offer three different options, even when the prisoner has failed to comply with the stipulated terms and conditions?

Does the prisoner still have the option of serving the remainder of his sentence at Kajang prison, being transferred to another prison designated by the commissioner-general of prisons, or serving the remainder of his sentence under house arrest at his own residence?
What sort of court order is that?
If this document is indeed genuine, as my source insists, I fully agree with the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) seeking clarification from the court.
There are simply too many errors, inconsistencies and ambiguities in the document to be ignored.
The attorney-general is right to have identified a potential conflict between the High Court’s order of release and the proposed house-arrest arrangement.

An order of release is intended to release a prisoner from custody. It is not an order to transfer a prisoner from one place of detention to another, even if Najib’s residence has been gazetted as a place of detention.
At the same time, the AGC cannot simply disregard a court order, whether it agrees with its contents or not.
The conflict and confusion may have arisen because Najib’s lawyers applied for and obtained what appears to be a conventional order of release, when his circumstances were anything but conventional.
His situation involved an unprecedented house-arrest arrangement that required a properly drafted and legally unambiguous court order.

This entire ordeal has been compounded by what appears to be the failure of a court official to produce a proper, concise and legally precise document in Bahasa Melayu, with clear terms and specific instructions.
Najib’s lawyers should have recognised this problem from the outset and ensured that the appropriate order was sought.

If the order of release is followed, and the AGC has no lawful grounds to refuse compliance with a court order, the consequence could be that Najib is released from his current detention and becomes liable to begin serving his 15-year prison sentence arising from his 1MDB conviction.
The irony is that this entire ordeal may have been caused by Najib’s own lawyers. It is therefore up to them to take the necessary steps to untangle the legal mess they may have created.
The court has a responsibility to issue a legally correct order, but the lawyers seeking that order have an equally important responsibility to ensure that they ask for the right one.
One thing should be made clear: the confusion and conflict are certainly not the king’s fault, nor should the attorney-general be blamed for seeking clarification.
The attorney general is right to insist that the matter be resolved carefully and in accordance with the law.
Given the public interest and constitutional implications, the AGC is also right to proceed cautiously. The eyes of all Malaysians are on this matter.
Ultimately, the law must prevail. Neither the court, the AGC nor the parties involved can afford to leave the public guessing about what the order actually means.
I believe the king and the Malaysian public would understand the need for such clarification.
What was supposed to be a straightforward court order has now become a full-blown court ordeal.
* This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.

e81c68b67844197d: DOHA, Nov 10 — Malaysia’s appointment as chair of Committee 5 at the 2026 International Telecommunication Union Plenipotentiary Conference (ITU PP-26) reflects the international community’s confidence in the country’s ability to play a neutral role in balancing the interests of various parties.
Committee 5 chair Eneng Faridah Iskandar said the appointment was not merely a personal recognition but a major achievement for Malaysia, according to a report published by Bernama.
“I think this is not only an achievement (but) actually an achievement for the country because Malaysia is seen as a neutral country that can accept the views of all parties.
“So, as chair, our task is to balance the interests and wishes of all parties, and we must be fair,” she told Bernama and RTM here today.

Eneng Faridah, who is also Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) Deputy Managing Director (Development), expressed her appreciation to the Malaysian government for having the confidence to nominate her for the role at the conference, which runs from November 9 to 27.
She said the position carried significant responsibility as she would not only represent Malaysia but also have to take into account the interests of all member states involved in the discussions.
Explaining Committee 5’s role, Eneng Faridah said the substantive committee was responsible for examining various policy and legal issues within the ITU framework.
More than 95 proposals covering over 40 resolutions have been submitted for discussion at this year’s conference.
“One of the main challenges is acting as an intermediary between various parties with different interests to reach a common agreement, as the ITU operates on the principle of consensus,” she said.
She said several preliminary meetings had been held ahead of the committee’s sessions, which are scheduled to begin tomorrow, to ensure that negotiations proceed smoothly.

One of the main committees at ITU PP-26, Committee 5, also known as the Policy and Legal Committee, is responsible for discussing proposed international telecommunications policies and regulations, as well as examining resolutions submitted by ITU member states.

Its chair plays a key role in conducting negotiations, balancing interests and bridging differences among member states to reach a consensus, before the committee’s deliberations are submitted to the conference for consideration and decisions.
PP-26, being held in Doha, is the ITU’s highest-level conference, convened every four years to determine the organisation’s direction, policies and strategic plans.
The Malaysian delegation to the conference is led by Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, with the mission of retaining the country’s seat on the ITU Council for the 2027-2030 term.

The ITU is a specialised agency of the United Nations (UN) responsible for information and communications technology (ICT), including setting global standards, allocating radio-frequency spectrum, coordinating satellites and efforts to bridge the global digital divide.

Lee said in his post that an LTA officer on a motorcycle had also spotted the same fawn, so they both reacted by separately alerting the relevant agencies — Animal Concerns Research and Education Society (ACRES) and the National Parks Board (NParks).
A video shared by Lee shows two NParks contractors lifting the fawn, with one of them carrying it into their response vehicle.
Two ACRES rescuers, a Land Transport Authority traffic marshal and crew from the Expressway Monitoring and Advisory System (EMAS) are also present at the scene.
Lee said the fawn’s mother was seen lying nearby and chased after the fawn from behind the fence as the vehicle drove off.
“Such a pitiful sight,” he wrote.
The motorcyclist said NParks officers informed him that they will usually release the fawn close to the original location where they are found, to facilitate reunion between the mammals.
Meanwhile, sharing an update, Save Sambar Deer said the fawn was brought to the Mandai Wildlife Centre for veterinary care.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Ongoing wildlife exclusion fencing works along the Bukit Timah Expressway. — Picture courtesy of Save Sambar Deer via AsiaOne
Fawn released after care
In response to AsiaOne’s queries, NParks and Mandai Nature, which operates Mandai Wildlife Centre, said the deer was found to be weak and severely dehydrated when it first arrived.

Veterinarians at Mandai Wildlife Centre, who are experienced with sambar and other deer species, carried out a full health assessment, including blood tests and radiographs, and began immediate treatment to stabilise it.

“After close monitoring overnight, the fawn showed improvement and was assessed to be suitable for release. It was released by NParks yesterday in a forested area near the location where it was found.”
The agencies reminded members of the public not to handle injured animals on their own.
They may contact NParks’ 24-hour Animal Response Centre at 1800-476-1600 for assistance. — AsiaOne

b0d98f1cf4989a1b: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — What began as a personal scandal involving one of Silicon Valley’s most powerful executives has become a crisis touching on corporate governance, national security and the global artificial intelligence industry.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s admission that he was unfaithful to his wife, Lori, has attracted widespread attention. But it is his reported relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based technology company Megaspeed, that has raised more serious questions.

According to The New York Times, US authorities investigated Alice Huang over suspicions that she had passed information to Beijing. China has rejected the espionage allegations, while Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets or US national security information have been compromised.
The financial fallout has been swift. Nvidia shares fell 4.3 per cent on Monday, erasing approximately US$190 billion (RM769.5 billion) from its market value, Reuters reported.
Here are five reasons the controversy matters beyond Huang’s private life.
1. National security enters the boardroom
Nvidia sits at the centre of Washington’s technological rivalry with Beijing, supplying advanced chips essential to developing powerful AI systems.
The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to target the Nvidia chief executive.
Reuters also reported that her former employer, Megaspeed, had faced scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Chinese customers obtain Nvidia chips subject to US export restrictions.

Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs has separately rejected reports that its officials investigated Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence links or relationship with Jensen Huang. However, Singapore police confirmed that investigations into Megaspeed were ongoing, CNA reported.

The allegations have also reached Congress. According to Reuters, three senior Republican lawmakers requested a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18 over Nvidia’s safeguards against foreign espionage.
Nvidia announced an independent investigation on November 8, while maintaining that it had no reason to believe sensitive company information or national security had been compromised.
2. A US$190 billion market shock
Few companies are as central to investor confidence in the AI boom as Nvidia.
Its processors power AI systems developed by some of the world’s biggest technology groups, making the chipmaker a major beneficiary of surging infrastructure spending.
According to Reuters, Nvidia shares closed 4.3 per cent lower on November 9, wiping approximately US$190 billion from its market capitalisation.
The sell-off followed the announcement of Nvidia’s investigation, although broader concerns about elevated AI valuations and the sustainability of the AI boom were already weighing on its shares.
The extent to which the scandal alone drove the decline remains unclear.
Nevertheless, the market reaction illustrates how uncertainty surrounding the leadership of a company worth trillions can translate into enormous losses in shareholder value.
3. The risks of a founder-led empire
Huang is more than Nvidia’s chief executive. He is the architect of its transformation from a graphics-chip specialist into an AI powerhouse.
His influence, industry relationships and public profile have become closely intertwined with Nvidia’s success.
Reuters has described Huang as one of the AI boom’s most prominent advocates, noting his celebrity-like standing, particularly in Asia.
That dependence creates what investors call key-person risk: the danger of a company relying too heavily on one individual.
The controversy consequently raises questions about succession planning, board independence and oversight, particularly when a founder’s reputation becomes inseparable from the business he built.
Nvidia, however, has stood behind Huang, saying he remains committed to leading the company without interruption.
4. A new headache in the US-China chip war
Huang has been an influential voice against sweeping US restrictions on semiconductor exports to China, arguing that they could accelerate Beijing’s development of rival technologies.
According to Reuters, he has cultivated close ties with US President Donald Trump while lobbying for greater access to the Chinese market.
The intelligence allegations risk complicating those efforts.
Trump said yesterday that he had spoken to Huang, who told him he had not known Alice Huang was allegedly working for Chinese intelligence.
The president also said the FBI was examining the matter, although he provided no further details.

For Nvidia, heightened political scrutiny could strengthen calls for tighter export controls, threatening its ability to balance commercial opportunities in China with Washington’s national security priorities.
5. Corporate transparency under scrutiny
An executive’s private life is generally not a boardroom matter. That changes when personal relationships potentially create business or national security risks.
In a November 8 message to employees, Huang acknowledged his infidelity and took responsibility for his actions, according to Reuters.
He also pledged to cooperate with Nvidia’s independent investigation.
The controversy took another turn on November 9 when Nvidia and Huang were named in a proposed shareholder class-action lawsuit in California.

According to Reuters, the complaint alleges that investors were misled because the company failed to disclose Huang’s reported relationship with Alice Huang and the potential national security concerns surrounding it.

The lawsuit, brought by shareholders led by Mark Kistenmacher, seeks unspecified damages. It was filed five minutes after the US stock market closed, meaning it did not trigger that day’s share-price decline.
The allegations remain unproven, but the case raises questions about when an executive’s personal conduct becomes material information for shareholders.

8c4f85be22873ce3: Au Kam San's international legal representative called the trial a ‘sham’ with ‘manufactured allegations’
Originally published on Global Voices
Au Kam San. Photo from Au Kam San's Facebook page.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Chinese territory of Macau recorded its first conviction under the city’s national security law on November 6, 2026, sentencing 69-year-old former lawmaker Au Kam San to 12.5 years in prison. The Macau Court of First Instance tried the case behind closed doors, and international observers and rights groups have criticized the verdict, calling it a “bogus prosecution” that included “serious violations of his right to a fair trial.” The case raises broader questions about how justice is carried out in Macau, and whether its courts offer a fair, open way to challenge the state.

Au served in Macau’s legislature for over 20 years and remained an outspoken current affairs commentator after his retirement in 2021. He was convicted on one count of subverting state power, three counts of contacting foreign organizations to endanger national security, and one count of violating confidentiality.
According to the court’s statement, the closed-door trial was held on September 16 and 18. Au was prosecuted under Macau’s domestic security law, enacted on March 3, 2009, and tightened in 2023.

He was accused of cooperating with hostile foreign organizations to collect and disseminate “numerous political propositions that were clearly permeated with [the intent of] subversion of state power” and to assist in the collection and dissemination of false information that intended to incite hatred against the central government, overthrow and undermine the fundamental national system established by the Chinese Constitution, cause foreign countries to take hostile actions against China and Macau, and disrupt the Macau Chief Executive election in 2024.
Au’s family members, several media outlets, and dozens of citizens attended the court’s public sentencing.

Au’s wife, Cheng Miu-shan, responded to the sentencing with an open letter, stating that the closed-door hearing and public sentencing were politically motivated and a baseless persecution to humiliate and smear her husband’s character.
Au’s daughter, Cherry Au, defended her father’s innocence in her interview with UK-based media outlet, the Independent:

“What saddens me the most is seeing him being portrayed as a villain by the very government that he served for so many years,” she said. “I hope people remember the person they knew throughout his career, the reason why they placed their trust in him and elected him time and again. Right now he is facing profound injustice. I hope those who remember his years of service will stand by him.”

Au Kam San has been detained since his arrest in July 2025. He was initially charged with three counts of “subverting state power,” three counts of “establishing contacts with organizations, groups or individuals outside the Macau Special Administrative Region to commit acts that endanger national security,” and one count of “violating confidentiality.” The court reduced the subversion charge to one count after the closed-door hearing.

After the public sentencing, the court issued a press release stressing that it appointed a lawyer to defend Au and that during the trial, Au did not dispute most of the facts and acknowledged that his collusion with and conspiracy with multiple overseas organizations constituted a crime.

It also pointed out that Au did not stop colluding with foreign and overseas organizations to subvert state power after the 2023 amendment of Macau national security law. The amendment has expanded the definition of subversive acts from “violent means” to “any illegal means,” to more closely align with Hong Kong’s 2020 version of national security law.
However, Au’s daughter told the press that her father had been barred from contacting his family and accessing a private lawyer to represent him in court.

Michael Polak, director of Justice Abroad, who has represented Au to submit an official complaint to the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, called Au’s trial a “sham” with “manufactured allegations” which brought Macau “in line with the most repressive state around the world, where the executive has the power to imprison those with whom it disagrees, with no semblance of a proper, fair legal process.”

In a statement following Au’s public sentencing, Polak also criticized that the private “hearing” had prevented any scrutiny of the Macao Authorities’ so-called evidence, thus creating a scenario where they could present anything, or nothing at all, to the Court and a conviction was inevitable.

So far, the public has not had any information about which foreign organizations, groups, or individuals Au Kam San conspired with to endanger national security and what distorted information he had spread to incite hatred against the Macau government, or undermine China’s socialist system.
The EU also issued a statement criticizing the conviction as “the erosion of political pluralism and freedom of speech” in Macau. It also expressed regret concerning the closed-door trial:
“We regret that access for the public, press and diplomats was restricted. After his arrest on July 30, 2025, Au Kam San had spent almost one year in incommunicado detention.”
Given that Au holds Portuguese citizenship, Polak called on Portugal and the EU to press for his release.

Au Kam San, a retired school teacher, is a prominent pro-democracy activist. After the 1989 pro-democracy movement, along with other pro-democracy figures such as António Ng Kuok Cheong, he established the “Macau Democratic Development Joint Committee” to “respond to the Chinese democratic movement and promote the democratic development of Macau.” They organized and participated in annual activities to commemorate China’s June 4, 1989, Tiananmen Square protests and massacre, until 2021, after the Macau authorities banned the Tiananmen vigil co-organized by Au, claiming that the event would incite state subversion.

Au started his public service career as a Macau municipal councilor from 1993 to 2001. In the first Legislative Council election after Macau’s reunification with China in 1999, Au and Ng formed a political team, “Democratic New Macau,” which won the race with 21 percent of the vote in their constituency. He was re-elected four times until 2021, when he announced his retirement. That year, the Election Committee disqualified 21 candidates from running in the legislative race, citing the Macau Court of Appeal ruling that supported Macau’s decision to ban commemoration of the June 4th Tiananmen Incident as subversive.

f60cbf1284a615ee: MIT researchers will lead an up to $53 million effort, awarded by the U.S. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) as part of its STREAM (Systems for Tracking and Resilience in Efficient Agricultural-input Management) program, to develop next-generation weed killers that help farmers and protect human health.  More than 1 billion pounds of herbicide are used in the United States every year. Herbicides help farmers by preventing significant crop loss due to weeds, and they enable regenerative farming practices that protect the soil, but some weeds are becoming resistant to the most common herbicides.  Exposure to herbicides may contribute to increased risk of cancer, metabolic and endocrine disorders, and other adverse health outcomes. Farm workers can be exposed from frequent herbicide use, but many U.S. residents are also exposed to these chemicals in small amounts through food and drinking water.  The MIT-led research team will develop new generative artificial intelligence tools to help them discover herbicide alternatives that are more effective and developed with human health in mind. Such alternatives could also help to reduce U.S. dependency on imported phosphorus, which is a critical ingredient in a major herbicide, glyphosate. “With herbicides like glyphosate and atrazine, there’s a real crisis because of resistance mutations that are coming,” says Christopher Voigt, head of MIT’s Department of Biological Engineering. “And if you combine the resistance mutations with issues around national security of the supply chain of the precursors to herbicides, we could find ourselves without these core agrochemicals that are absolutely essential for getting the high crop yields and economical prices that the United States now sees.” Voigt is the principal investigator for the project, known as Precision Learning for On-target Weed control (PLOW). The team is also expected to include researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, the University of Tennessee at Knoxville, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, and Robigo. The researchers are grouped into three teams that will tackle different aspects of the project, aligned with the STREAM Technical Areas. The generative AI group will develop models that can predict molecules — either chemical compounds or small interfering RNA (siRNA) — that disrupt the same plant enzymes targeted by glyphosate and other herbicides. Glyphosate kills weeds by interfering with an enzyme called EPSP synthase, which plants need to produce several critical amino acids. After many years of herbicide use, some weeds have begun to acquire genetic mutations that allow them to become resistant to those herbicides, which makes them less effective and poses a significant threat to crop yields. “There’s a real need for new herbicides because of resistance mutations that have been arising,” Voigt says. “There are also concerns about herbicides’ possible impacts on the environment and on humans, so it’s important to identify alternative ways of making herbicides, which as a general class of molecule are really critical to agriculture.” The MIT-led team plans to design generative AI models that will be able to predict molecules that can help prevent resistance from arising. The models will also optimize for other features such as low cost of synthesis, low risk of inducing resistance, and low risk of harming humans or causing ecological damage.  The group developing these AI models is led by Connor Coley, the Warren K. Lewis Associate Professor of Chemical Engineering at MIT; Regina Barzilay, the School of Engineering Distinguished Professor for AI and Health at MIT; and Alexander Tropsha, the K.H. Lee Distinguished Professor in the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy. The models are expected to generate billions of possible candidates, which will then be tested by a second research team. This high-throughput screening group will be led by Angela Koehler, the Charles W. and Jennifer C. Johnson Professor of Biological Engineering at MIT, and Jaime Cheah, the associate director of scientific outreach and collaborative screening in the Center for the Development of Therapeutics at the Broad Institute. “Those libraries will be screened both to identify those molecules that hit their target, but also to then provide all of that screening data back to the computational approach in order to improve it,” Voigt says. Once the candidate pools are narrowed down, researchers on a third team will begin greenhouse studies to evaluate how each molecule performs under different agricultural conditions. That team will be led by Neal Stewart and Scott Lenaghan, co-directors of the Center for Agricultural Synthetic Biology at UTK; Patrick Tranel, the Tom and Peggy Ainsworth Professor of Crop Sciences at the University of Illinois; Tim Willson, the Harold Kohn Distinguished Professor at the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy; and Andee Wallace PhD ’20, CEO and founder of Robigo.  The first greenhouse tests of initial RNAi candidates are expected to be complete by the end of the first year of the program. As part of this project, the research team will also develop living microbial systems that degrade agrochemicals before they reach food, soil, or waterways. Engineered bacteria, fungi, and srRNA will convert chemicals and formulation ingredients into biomass, providing a scalable strategy to reduce environmental and human exposure. This research is funded by the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) under agreement number 140D042690030. 73bd9174dba5f064: BEIJING, Nov 10 — China’s trade surplus ballooned to more than US$1 trillion (RM4.06 trillion) in October, official data showed today, reaching the milestone even earlier than last year’s record-breaking surge in overseas shipments.

Exports from the world’s second-largest economy have surged in recent months, driven in part by soaring global demand for artificial intelligence-related products including computer chips, data centre servers and networking equipment.
The trade boom has offered Beijing a key economic lifeline as domestic activity is weighed by longstanding woes in the once-roaring property sector.
Exports jumped 35.2 per cent year-on-year to US$412.3 billion last month, according to the General Administration of Customs, while imports in October expanded 41.6 per cent to US$307.1 billion.
That brought China’s total trade surplus during the first 10 months to a towering US$1.04 trillion, according to the GAC.
The country is well on track to surpass the record US$1.2 trillion hit last year, when the US$1 trillion mark was reached in November.
However, the export boom has fuelled tensions with several key trading partners, who worry that floods of lower-cost Chinese goods are crowding out local competition.
Exports to the United States surged 32.9 per cent last month, the GAC data showed.
The figures come ahead of another high-stakes meeting between President Xi Jinping and US counterpart Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China next week.
The two have navigated a shaky truce to a fierce trade war since their meeting in October of 2025.
The Apec gathering runs from November 18 to 19 in Shenzhen and could also see a trilateral between Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. — AFP
23d7b6245637e5ff: HONG KONG, Nov 10 — Asian stocks rallied today to extend a Wall Street surge led by technology firms as investors took advantage of lower prices following last week’s rout, while another plunge in oil prices added to the upbeat mood.
AI-linked firms led gains across the region, in stark contrast to the battering in reaction to last Tuesday’s Democratic sweep of Congress that stoked regulatory concerns.

However, traders remain on edge about profitability in light of the vast sums pumped into the sector, while they were also keeping tabs on Nvidia after boss Jensen Huang’s admission of an affair amid speculation of a Chinese espionage plot.

Titans including Amazon, Microsoft and Apple were among the big gainers yesterday in New York as tech bounced back with help from bargain-hunting, with observers pointing out that confidence in the AI outlook remained solid.
The Nasdaq’s 2.7 per cent spike led a strong day on Wall Street, and Asian investors took up the baton.

Seoul surged more than five per cent at one point thanks to similar advances for chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung, while Tokyo jumped almost three per cent on the back of strong performances by Kioxia, SoftBank and Tokyo Electron.
Taiwan’s TSMC rallied more than one per cent and MediaTek more than seven per cent to drag the Taiex 3.5 per cent higher.
Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Manila and Wellington were also higher.
However, SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes said the gains did not suggest markets were back in rude health.
“The market rallied because the sellers stepped away, not because the entire buy-side suddenly rediscovered its courage,” he wrote in a commentary.

“For the second consecutive session, the companies receiving the enormous capital expenditure cheques dramatically outperformed the businesses writing them. That is a potentially important development after last week’s indiscriminate liquidation,” he said.
‘Positive momentum’
“The hyperscalers remain central to the AI investment cycle, but the market is increasingly questioning the returns on the extraordinary sums being committed to new infrastructure.

“Equipment providers, optical networking companies and selected data-centre suppliers can still benefit from existing spending programmes, even as investors become more selective about the ultimate economics for the companies funding those projects.”
Oil prices continued their retreat on hopes the US and Iran will eventually bring an end to the Middle East crisis.
Both main contracts fell around one per cent today, extending the previous day’s drop that saw Brent give up almost six per cent.
They have lost around 20 per cent this month as traders bet on a resolution to the seven-month-old conflict, which has sent inflation soaring and forced central banks to hike interest rates.
US President Donald Trump said yesterday there was “positive momentum” toward ending the war after meeting Qatar’s prime minister at the White House.
“I had an excellent conversation with Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani,” Trump said on Truth Social, adding that “much was discussed with respect to the Islamic Republic of Iran”.
While expectations had grown ahead of last week’s midterms that he would resume strikes on Iran this month, Trump has talked down such a move while leaving the door open to them.

In his post yesterday, Trump reiterated that the US was “locked and loaded,” but that he believed further strikes were “quite unlikely” given that key US allies in the Gulf “would prefer the status quo”.
His comments echoed early statements to CNN over the weekend when he said it was “highly unlikely” fighting would resume.

97a341dab0d8388a: NEW YORK, Nov 10 — Boeing will cut about five per cent of its commercial plane workforce as it moderates the pace of ramping up jet production, the company said yesterday.

The company will eliminate the posts through a mix of layoffs and attrition because of a slower ramp-up to “provide our factories and supply chain partners additional time to achieve stability,” said a message to employees from Boeing commercial chief Stephanie Pope.
“Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position,” she added.
Pope praised the team for improved operations reflected in US certifications this year of the 737 MAX 7 and 737 MAX 10.

“While we have made substantial progress, we have not yet fully recovered,” said Pope, who promised to treat employees with “dignity and respect” as the company moves ahead with layoff notifications beginning in December.

Boeing executives had previously signalled slower plans to raise plane output, saying in a late October conference call the company would no longer meet its target for 2026 deliveries and that it had pushed back the timeframe for lifting 737 MAX production to 52 from 47 until the second half of 2027.

Raising 737 MAX output has been viewed by investors as central to revenue and profit growth after a long period of financial losses due to safety problems, including two deadly MAX crashes in 2018 and 2019.
“We’re making progress, but we still have more work to do, and I’m expecting it’ll take us into next year to get fully stable at this rate,” CEO Kelly Ortberg said October 27.
Ortberg cited the need for greater predictability in wing production and with the production of fuselages at its Kansas operation.
Shares of Boeing were down less than 0.1 per cent after midday. — AFP
858ba641b68502cf: Cisco will no longer create products that don’t integrate with Cloud Control, its SaaS-y management platform that offers netadmins a single tool to manage all of the networking giant’s devices and much of its software portfolio.

The networking giant announced Cloud Control in June 2025 and only made it available to customers in the USA. Cisco has previously told The Register that slow rollout reflects the fact that Cisco needs to nail privacy and other regulatory niceties, and deploy infrastructure, before introducing the service to other markets.

It appears Cisco is now satisfied it has sorted out those issues. Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing, today told the company’s Live conference in Australia that Cloud Control will come online in the European Union, UK, and Down Under in February 2027. Japan, India, and Canada will get their turn in May.
Schultz said Cisco is “working tirelessly” to deploy Cloud Control across the world as soon as possible.
He also revealed that, starting next year, Cisco will no longer ship products that don’t integrate with Cloud Control.

That doesn’t mean those products will be manageable only if they can connect to Cloud Control. Instead, the decision reflects Cisco’s belief that the main thing stopping its customers buying more of its products is the complexity of operating them in concert. Schultz also feels that Cloud Control represents “platform advantage” for Cisco, because when users integrate networking, security, and observability the result is better manageability and resilience.

Schultz also told the conference that Cisco will bundle its Thousand Eyes observability and security tool with the “Essentials” and “Advantage” licenses. “We admit it was hard to license and deploy,” he said during his keynote speech, adding that the tool will be deployed automatically with Wi‑Fi 6E and Wi‑Fi 7 hardware.

Another product Cisco plans to bring to more customers is Live Protect, a tool that implements compensating controls for flaws that organizations can’t immediately patch. The product has become particularly useful since Anthropic's Mythos model, and similar AI offerings, made it possible to quickly find more software bugs and flaws and overwhelmed tech teams whose patching apparatus was not set up to handle hundreds of montly CVEs.

Live Protect currently works on some of Cisco's datacenter switches, plus SD-WAN and WLAN controllers. From December, Cisco will extend it to 8000 series routers, secure firewalls, campus gateway, and to Cloud Control itself. From May 2027, Live Protect will work with Cisco’s ASR 9000 series service aggregation routers and Network Convergence System.
"Expect this to be a major investment area," Schultz added. ®

3188493d3ae00f89: SINGAPORE: Singapore has launched a gold vaulting service for overseas central banks and official institutions, seeking to capitalise on global demand to diversify storage of bullion reserves.

Gold will be stored in the city-state’s national currency vault, which has capacity for as much as 500 tonnes, with room to expand as demand grows, the Monetary Authority of Singapore said in a statement on Tuesday.

“Singapore does not aim to replace other gold centres and gold vaulting services,” MAS chairman Gan Kim Yong, who is also the country’s deputy prime minister, told reporters. “With the growing demand for gold as a reserve asset, I think central banks are also looking for alternatives, looking for more options to strengthen their resilience in terms of their gold reserves,” he said.
MAS will also offer gold custody accounts to select Singapore-based bullion banks with expertise in providing the services, the central bank said in the statement.

The latest push by Singapore comes amid heightened demand for gold from both institutional investors and central banks, which have accumulated the metal at a rapid pace in recent years as geopolitical tensions and concerns over government debt boost its appeal as a haven and a way to diversify investment portfolios.

cf8c04cdcf6fc894: BEIJING: China's trade surplus surged past US$1 trillion in the first 10 months as a global race to build AI infrastructure buoyed sales of high-tech products and helped offset weak domestic demand, a dynamic likely to sharpen tensions with major trading partners.

The figures highlight Beijing's growing reliance on overseas demand to support an economy hobbled by subdued consumption and a protracted property slump. But while the global AI investment boom is expected to keep demand for Chinese technology products strong into 2027, it risks deepening domestic imbalances and fuelling trade frictions with partners including the EU.

Exports rose sharply by 35.2% in October from the same month last year in US dollar terms, customs data showed on Tuesday, only a touch slower than the 36.3% surge in September, but ahead of economists' forecast for an increase of 33.5%.
That helped lift China's trade surplus to US$1.04 trillion in the first 10 months, topping US$1 trillion for a second consecutive year and reaching the milestone a month earlier than in 2025.

The swelling surplus could fuel further tensions with the European Union, where leaders have called for more trade curbs with China after reaching an agreement with Beijing to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc over the next few years. Because the measures have yet to take effect, factories are expected to bring forward shipments, bolstering exports in the near term.

China on Monday officially announced the extension of a trade truce with Washington due to expire on Nov 10 by two months, but said last week that expanding its purchases of US farm goods would hinge on the implementation of their agreed reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement.

"The risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will remain elevated in 2027, particularly as Chinese manufacturers continue expanding their presence in overseas markets," said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China.
Imports grew 41.6%, beating the median forecast for a 32% increase in the Reuters poll and accelerating from the 31% growth in September.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit will take place next week in the southern Chinese tech and innovation hub Shenzhen, where Chinese president Xi Jinping and US president Donald Trump are expected to meet for the third time so far this year.
One big worry for Beijing is that consumers remain reluctant to spend, constrained by a property market downturn that has battered household wealth and dented confidence in the economic outlook.

Sluggish demand at home has pushed Chinese automakers to seek sales in overseas markets. China's car exports maintained a solid pace of growth in October, while domestic vehicle sales recorded a 12th straight month of declines, separate data released by an industry association showed.
Greater reliance on exports, however, leaves China's economy increasingly exposed to any slowdown in global demand.
Much of the strength in exports this year has been fuelled by a global push to expand AI infrastructure.

"The outlook for exports depends on how long the AI boom will last," Macquarie analysts wrote. They expect China's exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before starting to slow from the first quarter of 2027.

3fde928bb7a7ca6f: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 10 — Anthropic announced yesterday that it would release updated versions of two of its most powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models as the company prepares for a highly anticipated IPO this month.
The new models, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, can perform up to 30 per cent faster than previous versions, particularly on complex tasks such as coding, while costing 20 per cent less, the company said.
Both are built on the same underlying model. Fable 5.2 has safeguards that block most cybersecurity and biology tasks, which lets Anthropic offer it to all users.
Mythos 5.2 has fewer of those restrictions and is available only to vetted organisations working in cybersecurity or biomedical research.
The first versions of Fable and Mythos were released under a cloud of controversy.

Both models were pulled days after their June launch, when the US Commerce Department, citing national security concerns, ordered Anthropic to bar access by foreign nationals. The controls were lifted weeks later.

The latest versions come as Anthropic is aiming to hold its initial public offering the week of November 16, when it is expected to raise up to US$100 billion (RM405 billion), which would make it the largest IPO on record.
The San Francisco-based lab’s Wall Street debut is expected to fetch a valuation exceeding US$1 trillion, though estimates have fallen in recent weeks from a high of US$2 trillion.
The stock market debut is being seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom lifting the US economy can last.
Growth has been staggering at the company. Anthropic’s revenue reached US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from just US$1.4 billion a year earlier, a securities filing showed earlier this month.
Sales growth slowed from previous quarters, however, amid fierce competition from ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and cheaper models, many of them from China.
Anthropic also posted an operating loss of US$567 million in the third quarter as it paid more for short-term computing capacity.
The company’s valuation has also been weighed down by a broader market pullback after a string of quarterly earnings reports spooked investors.
These raised concerned about the hundreds of billions of dollars that US tech giants are spending on AI.

e84f1d485d7d4933: NEW YORK, Nov 10 — AI chip behemoth Nvidia was plunged into turmoil yesterday after CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged having an affair, with reports saying US officials believe the woman was spying for China.
Beijing denied the claim, but shares of the chipmaker tumbled after Nvidia’s board opened an inquiry into reports that Huang had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Nvidia shares closed more than four per cent lower, after being down nearly nine per cent earlier in the session.

Late last month, The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials had determined Alice Huang, a Chinese executive linked to Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, had been funnelling information to Beijing.
The executive, also known as Huang Le and no relation to 63-year-old Taiwanese-born Jensen Huang, developed a close relationship with him, the Times said.
In a message to Nvidia employees released on Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife.
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he said.

Jensen Huang is a central figure in the AI boom and a close informal adviser to US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly opposed regulating the industry so as not to let China gain the upper hand.
Trump told reporters that he had spoken with Nvidia’s chief yesterday and that he was “suffering greatly.”
“I asked him that question, ‘did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him,” Trump told a White House press briefing.
The Times said Alice Huang’s relationship with the Nvidia chief could have given her insights into Trump’s thinking around AI.
Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing Monday that “the narrative of a so-called Chinese spy is entirely baseless vilification and smearing.”
AI is likely to come up when Trump meets President Xi Jinping later this month at a summit in China.
‘You never know’
Asked Sunday whether Huang would join the president’s Asia trip, which includes the Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen, Trump told reporters: “I don’t know but I’ll certainly take him.”
Nvidia’s board said in a statement Sunday it had opened an independent probe “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
“While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” it said.
China is in a race for tech dominance against the United States, which restricts the export to China of the most cutting-edge silicon chips.
Nvidia, a global leader in producing chips used to train and run AI models, is one of the world’s most valuable companies.
Megaspeed was under scrutiny for possibly steering Nvidia AI chips to China, the Times report said, citing unnamed sources briefed on the matter.
Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about Huang’s relationship with the businesswoman roughly a year ago and chose not to act on the information, the Times report said.
Trump said Sunday that he did not regret not acting on this intelligence, calling Huang “an honourable guy.”
‘Black eye moment’
Technology analyst Dan Ives, with the investment bank Yorkville Ives, said the inquiry was “a black eye moment” for Jensen Huang.
He predicted it would at the very least spark multiple congressional inquiries and “create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons.”
In the near term, Huang is expected to keep his job but risks being removed as Nvidia’s CEO depending on the findings of the inquiry, Ives said.

George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, told AFP “it would be premature to conclude that Jensen poses a threat to US national security before the facts are fully established.”
“Once you become famous, you will naturally become a target,” Chen said.

The House Select Committee on China last week asked Huang to appear in Washington on November 18 for a “closed-door briefing on Nvidia’s security protocols,” according to a letter posted on X that cited reports about Alice Huang. — AFP

Maka, dengan sendirinya semua penghuni yang sememangnya tinggal di banglo mewah di Langgak Duta kekal sebagai penghuni. Ertinya, Rosmah Mansor, isteri Najib, bersama anggota keluarga terdekat akan bersama Najib dalam 'penjara' Langgak Duta. Begitu juga pembantu rumah dan sebagainya (kalau ada).

350cd2b042e00eb8: SINGAPORE, Nov 9 — SoftBank Group Corp and Grab Holdings Ltd yesterday announced the signing of joint development agreements in connection with plans for US$1.85 billion (RM7.5 billion) initial combined seed capital to develop artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure in Malaysia with Petroleum Sarawak Bhd (Petros).

“The collaboration aimed to establish AI infrastructure in Malaysia to meet the growing demand for computing capacity across Southeast Asia and globally.

“Once fully operational, the facilities are expected to be amongst the largest AI infrastructure of their kind in Asia, providing governments, multinational companies and small businesses with reliable access to advanced computing capabilities,” they said.
According to the statement, the proposed investment will be deployed in stages subject to projects achieving key development and customer contract milestones, and the necessary closing conditions.

Grab co-founder, chairman and chief executive officer Anthony Tan said the company and SoftBank plan to build critical AI infrastructure in Malaysia, where Grab began, for all of Southeast Asia region.
“This infrastructure will allow us to accelerate the development of localised AI solutions for our communities.

The facilities will operate in line with Malaysia’s renewable energy use guidelines, and feature high-efficiency infrastructure designed to reduce water use and reliance on local power grids.

42bc912dc85d4181: Seperti parti politik di mana-mana negara termasuklah Malaysia, mempunyai parti yang memperjuangkan berbagai ideologi. Dengan ideologi ini mereka mencari pengikut. Nasionalisme, sosialisme, sekularisme termasuklah membawa idealisme agama. Fahaman ini disebar kepada rakyat agar menyokong agenda mereka yang mereka percaya terbaik untuk semua.

Tetapi, dalam usaha mengekalkan sokongan, manipulasi tetap berlaku. Paling sedap guna agama. Alasan, dalil dan nas dipakai untuk mencari kelebihan ataupun menutup kelemahan sendiri. Pahala, dosa, syurga dan neraka dijadikan modal niaga untuk mengabsahkan tindakan mereka.

Seorang pemimpin politik sebuah parti agama dalam ceramahnya beberapa minggu lalu menjawab kritikan mengapa negeri yang ditadbir oleh mereka selama 36 tahun lambat maju dengan jawapan yang mudah. "Kita bukannya nabi." Senang, kan?

Pasti penyokong mereka terpesona dan kagum dengan jawapan itu. Tiada yang benar melainkan benar belaka hujah itu. Betullah tu, kita bukan nabi, kata penyokong mereka. Kita tak sempurna. Tetapi, bila kerajaan persekutuan atau kerajaan negeri lain yang ditadbir oleh musuh politik mereka lambat, dalam hal banjir di Selangor misalnya apa yang penyokong mereka tak hentam? Kenapa tak letak hujah pemimpin kamu itu kepada keadaan pihak lain?
"Benda bukan boleh selesai sehari dua, kita bukan nabi, kan?"

Terbaru, minggu lalu seorang lagi pemimpin parti itu dalam hantaran yang dibuatnya di Facebook menulis orang yang menderma untuk membantu bekas perdana menteri Najib Razak membayar denda RM50 juta boleh mendapat pahala. Beliau mengaitkan sumbangan itu dan segala bantuan berkaitan dengannya adalah usaha memudahkan urusan. Memudahkan urusan orang dapat pahala. Peh!

Kenyataan ini sangatlah menarik. Bukanlah sebab kita baru sahaja mengetahui bahawa menderma merupakan amalan yang baik dalam Islam. Sejak kecil kita sudah diajar begitu. Masukkan duit ke dalam tabung masjid, bantu anak yatim, beri makan orang miskin, semuanya amalan mulia. Tangan yang di atas lebih baik daripada tangan di bawah. Semua itu telah kita belajar.

Tetapi, apabila derma dikaitkan dengan seorang tokoh politik yang telah disabitkan kesalahan oleh mahkamah, persoalannya menjadi sedikit berbeza. Adakah setiap amalan derma yang kita buat kepada semua pihak itu sama nilainya? Itu yang lebai-lebai politik harus ajar pengikutnya. Selain nilai dan jumlah, perlu dididik juga tujuan sesuatu sumbangan itu apakah ia benar-benar dituntut dalam agama. Apakah ia membantu permasalahan ummah? Apakah akan memberi kebaikan dan keberkatan kepada bangsa, agama dan negara? Dari segi keadilan sejagat, apakah tindakan ini sesuai?

Maaflah, saya tak boleh terima bab seorang ahli politik merasakan dia ada autoriti untuk menentukan seseorang itu boleh mendapat pahala atau dosa. Kalau tolong pihak mereka, dapat pahala. Kalau buat perkara yang sama untuk pihak lain, berdosa. Sewaktu bermusuh habis semua pihak bergelumang dosa. Bila berbaik, kutip dalil untuk menyucikannya. Jika tempat orang ditimpa banjir itu murka Allah, jika tempat mereka kena, itu ujian. Ini amat memalukan jika kita fikir dengan akal yang waras. Saya mahu bertanya, ke mana penyokong kamu hendak dibawa? Barangkali ada segelintir penyokong parti kamu yang berasa malu juga dengan kenyataan ini.

Soal dosa pahala ini bukan perkara yang sedap-sedap jadi bahan mainan. Dalam kehidupan beragama, pahala dan dosa merupakan antara asas yang membentuk pertimbangan manusia. Orang melakukan kebaikan dengan mengharapkan ganjaran tuhan, manakala menjauhi kejahatan kerana takut akan balasan-Nya. Tapi mengapa bagi kamu, pahala dibuat seperti mata ganjaran untuk tebus barang di kedai serbaneka. Kita jadi ahli kedai, dapat kad keahlian, kemudian jika ada tawaran promosi, kita pun beli barang. Daripada pembelian barang, kita dapat 'point' (pahala) yang boleh ditebus kemudiannya. Macam itu? Gila betul.

Begini, biar saya jelaskan. Dalam isu duit denda Najib, saya boleh faham jika ada penyokongnya yang bersungguh-sungguh mahu membantu beliau. Dalam politik, kesetiaan atau ketaasuban bukan sesuatu yang pelik. Semua parti ada penyokong fanatik. Mereka akan bermati-matian mempertahankan pemimpin mereka. Dan dalam isu Najib ini, ada juga yang bersimpati terhadapnya dan ada juga yang mengenang jasa ketika beliau berkuasa lalu mereka pun menderma. Itu hak mereka. Pemimpin parti lain, jika kalah saman pun akan ada penyokong mereka yang bantu buat kutipan dana.

Tetapi, mengusik sentimen penyokong dengan mempergunakan ganjaran pahala ini agak teruk, bagi saya jika kita fikir dalam-dalam. Apakah boleh kita guna 'fatwa' yang sama untuk kutip derma dan permudahkan urusan ratusan bekas banduan yang sudah bebas supaya urusan mereka dipermudahkan? Mereka terpaksa bergelut kesusahan dalam mendapat pekerjaan. Di mana seruan buat pahala kamu? Apakah manusia seperti mereka tak berguna di mata kamu? Bukankah mereka juga berhak kembali ke pangkuan masyarakat untuk menyumbang bakti dan tenaga? Kenapa berpilih-pilih? Di mana keadilannya kalau begitu?

Di luar sana, berapa ramai orang yang memerlukan bantuan untuk membayar kos rawatan, membeli keperluan sekolah anak atau menyelesaikan hutang akibat kesempitan hidup? Berapa ramai rakyat memerlukan air bersih di rumah? Apa usaha dan inisiatif kamu untuk memudahkan urusan mereka? Takkan kepada marhaen asyik dijual pahala dan syurga sahaja demi nak menutup kemalasan kamu berkhidmat? Jika kamu sebagai pentadbir negeri bekerja keras memberikan kemudahan urusan rakyat di bawah kamu, bukankah kamu juga akan mendapat pahala yang besar? Tapi kamu berhelah, 'kita bukan nabi'. Ini sangat teruk!

Apabila seorang ahli politik memakai jubah dan kopiah bercakap tentang pahala, kenyataannya tentulah akan diterima oleh penyokong mereka. Apatah lagi seseorang ahli politik itu mempunyai latar belakang pendidikan agama atau berasal daripada keluarga ulama yang dihormati. Itu akan jadi lebih kuat.

Tetapi, ayuhlah berfikir secara realistik, kita memang tidak tahu apakah dapat pahala atau tidak jika seseorang itu menderma kepada Najib. Jika dapat pun kita tak tahu bagaimana bentuknya, besar mana atau apa rupanya. Itu bukan kita yang tentukan.

Pemimpin yang fatanah seharusnya lebih tahu memilih perkataan sesuai dalam menyampaikan maksudnya. Tetapi, dek kerana miskin kata-kata dan hujah, maka modal niaga paling sesuai ialah menjual agama dan meletakkan pahala di atas meja. Apakah ahli politik merasakan bahawa tuhan memberikan mereka kuasa juga dalam mengagih pahala?
"Kepada sesiapa yang hendak menderma kepada Najib, dibolehkan kerana itu hak anda. Bersimpati, menolong dan memudahkan urusan orang lain adalah amalan yang digalakkan."
Hah! Saya rasa ayat sebegitu sudah cukup. Nampaklah bijak tanpa menanggalkan ciri ‘keustazannya’, kan?

Dalam sinis, saya tetap menganggap menjual pahala dan dosa dalam permainan politik adalah menghina kebijaksanaan rakyat. Kalau ahli politik pun boleh menentukan siapa dapat pahala, alamatnya selepas ini manifesto pilihan raya mungkin tidak lagi menjanjikan pembangunan, pekerjaan atau kos sara hidup yang lebih rendah. Cukuplah dengan janji pahala atau menggunakan alasan 'kita bukan nabi' seperti alasan seorang lagi pemimpin politik parti yang sama.
Malulah sikit. Kalau tak malu dengan tuhan, malulah sikit dengan segelintir penyokong parti kamu sendiri yang lebih bijak daripada kamu. Takkan kamu nampak mereka semua lekeh daripada kamu?
