70bbc1169fd03a37: Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave.

World models are used to train physical AI systems like robots how to navigate the real world. They predict the consequences of actions. But they do so based on observed data. These models could provide better direction to robots if they were able to make inferences about possible actions without being trained for all the possible outcomes.

Randall Balestriero (Brown University, AMI Labs), Kerda Varaku, and Turing Award winner Yann LeCun (NYU, AMI Labs) describe an approach that might allow that to happen in a pre-print paper, "Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus."

The Latin refers to Gottfried Leibniz's axiom "nature makes no leaps," which had a good run until it ran headlong into quantum mechanics. Yet for the authors, the saying explains how they have been able to devise a method for zero-shot physics inference.

Counterfactual world models, said Balestriero in an email to The Register use "the mismatch between your prediction and the real world to figure out what did you get wrong, and from that you can better understand what happened for better future predictions, debugging, reasoning, all at test time."

Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models, developed by LeCun and colleagues back in 2023, have been proposed for robots because they can take an action as input and ask what the world would be like with that action.

But a JEPA world model produces an average of outcomes and would not be able to anticipate counterfactual scenarios – events that didn't happen. The technique that the researchers developed is not specific to JEPAs – it can be applied to any world model that predicts the average next state under any action. But JEPA models are particularly well suited to being adapted.

Balestriero said that the counterfactual world model experiments were done using off-the-shelf encoders (DINOv2 and MAE) without any fine-tuning and only a small predictor trained on top. Creating a counterfactual world model from that starting point would only require minor additions.
Counterfactual world models predict alternative scenarios more effectively by inferring possibilities from what did occur.

"In causal inference, answering 'What would have happened had I acted differently?' takes three steps," explained Balestriero. "You use what you observed to learn something about those hidden factors, you change the action, and you predict again with the hidden factors kept exactly as they were.
"Our counterfactual world model does all three steps with one subtraction."
Balestriero cited an example from the paper: a boat crossing a river with a hidden current and how the JEPA world model and counterfactual world model predicted the boat's movements.

"The world model predicted where the boat would end up after steering left, and it actually ended up two meters further downstream," he explained. "Those two meters are the signature of the current that occurred. To answer 'where would the boat be had I steered right?', we take the world model's prediction for steering right and add the same two meters. In other words, the counterfactual is what actually happened, plus the difference between the model's predictions for the alternative action and for the action taken.

"Physics enters to justify this rule, not as an equation the model fits. Over a short time, the effect of the action and the effect of the current each grow in proportion to the duration, while their interaction grows only with its square, so over short steps they simply add up, like forces.

"We prove that the fraction of the disturbance's effect that this rule gets wrong shrinks with the square of the time step, and that no method using the same ordinary data can do better than this rate in the worst case."
Counterfactual world models have three likely uses, according to Balestriero. The first is having a robot retry an action after a surprise event.

"When an attempt fails because of something the robot could not see, such as an unexpected load, a current or a weak motor, the counterfactual world model lets it estimate which action would have worked in that same situation," he explained. "In our simulated tasks, choosing the action this way reaches the goal in 35 to 69 percent of events, against 14 to 23 percent for a planner that knows the true simulator but ignores the observed outcome. With two more attempts on the same event, success rises to 51 to 97 percent."
He also sees these models being useful for adapting to persistent fault, like a miscalibrated motor, and helping people understand failures.

"World models are trained to predict, and they are getting good at it," said Balestriero. "But a robot, a car or a drone acting in the real world is constantly surprised by things it could not see coming. After a surprise, the useful question is no longer what was expected, but what would have happened had it acted differently in that same situation. You need that answer to debug a failure, to tell a bad decision from bad luck, or to decide what to do on the next attempt, and prediction alone does not provide it."

The researchers initial attempts to address the issue involved adding a learned component to the world model that infers whatever hidden disturbance (e.g. the current in the boat scenario) affected the anticipated outcome. But that approach was too fragile.

"Trying to understand why led to the theory," explained Balestriero. "Learning the disturbance from ordinary data is not just hard, it is impossible in general: the hidden noise can be relabeled differently for each action without changing a single prediction, so the data cannot tell you which labeling is the right one. The missing piece has to come from outside the data. For physical systems, it comes from the fact that forces add and that their interaction builds up slowly in time. Once you accept that, the learned disturbance model becomes unnecessary: the gap between what happened and what was predicted already carries the information you need, and you carry it over to the other action."
Balestriero said that control engineers have been implementing corrections of this sort for decades, to tune hand-built models.

"What was missing was why the same correction is justified for learned world models that see the world through images, what can and cannot be recovered without paired data, and where it breaks," he said. "The paper answers these questions by connecting causal inference, control and world models. The title comes from Leibniz's law of continuity, natura non facit saltus, 'nature makes no leaps,' which is precisely the property that makes all of this work."
The researchers' paper was provided to The Register prior to its release on ArXiv. It is expected to be released this week. ®

6f2117f6f58d050d: Windows testers are getting a new option in the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs – one to banish the pop-ups without needing to venture deep into Settings.

It's only taken several decades for Microsoft to put the off switch where the interruption actually happens. The accessibility features themselves are useful, though triggering their activation prompts by accident is another matter.

Once enabled, Sticky Keys let users press modifier keys (such as Control) one at a time instead of holding them down together. For example, rather than holding Control and pressing C to copy, a user can press and release Control, then press C. Filter Keys, meanwhile, ignores brief or repeated keystrokes and adjusts the keyboard's repeat behavior.

However, the dialogs are of little use to people who don't need the features, and they can pop up at the most inconvenient moments. Tap Shift five times, and you'll see what we mean: Windows chimes and shows a dialog asking whether you'd like to turn on Sticky Keys. Dismiss it, hit Shift five times, and there it is again.
Or hold down the right Shift key for eight seconds to be treated to the Filter Keys pop-up.

You can stop this behavior elsewhere in the system, but it requires a trek through Windows settings. The change, introduced in the Experimental Windows Insider Build 26340.9882, adds an option to the Sticky Keys or Filter Keys dialogs to dismiss the prompts permanently.
It's a small change, but one that should spare users an irritating interruption. Better late than never – even if "never ask me again" has taken roughly three decades to reach the dialog.
Former Microsoft engineer Charles Opperman said he wrote the dialog in early 1995 "after @bradsilverberg kids kept activating StickeyKeys [sic] while playing Space Cadet pinball."

Opperman added that a link to Settings was added in Windows 98 or what would become Windows 2000, and a checkbox was considered even then, but it wasn't deemed a priority. Users could turn off the prompt via settings. Now the option is front and center.
The option is also rolling out in the Windows Insider Beta channel, although Microsoft has not announced a general release date. ®
1a04107834027bb8: NASA is moving ahead with its plan to repurpose a Mars rover engineering model as a lunar trundlebot for less than $400 million.

The robot, dubbed PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration), is a cut-and-shut of engineering test articles used for the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers, currently rolling around the Red Planet.

During a weekend briefing, NASA outlined the plan for PROMISE: to land the robot on the lunar surface by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. PROMISE will be preceded by NASA's VIPER trundlebot, which is expected to survive only 100 days on the Moon's surface. PROMISE will carry copies of VIPER's science instruments, including a drill capable of boring 1 meter into the lunar regolith.

Power will come from a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) left over from the Cassini mission. NASA acknowledged the fuel was processed some time ago – the Cassini mission to Saturn was launched in 1997 – but anticipates there will be plenty of heat and power for PROMISE's components.

Blue Origin is to deposit the rover on the Moon. NASA awarded the company a $94 million base contract, "with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole."

The figures make it difficult to ascertain the exact cost of the PROMISE mission. However, during the briefing, NASA said it had "a pretty firm agreement with JPL to basically deliver the rover to the surface under $400 million." The $400 million includes the lander, which will be Blue Origin's Mark 1.

Earlier this year, The Planetary Society's chief of space policy, Casey Drier, estimated that the mission (including repurposing the hardware developed for Mars and landing it on the Moon) would cost at least $723 million. At the time, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said: "if PROMISE costs even 20 percent of your low-end estimate, we simply will not fly it."
Assuming Isaacman was only talking about the rover, Drier's figure drops to $489 million without launch and landing costs. 20 percent of that is… not going to be enough.

That also doesn't account for the impact of taking away the hardware built for the Mars program. During the briefing, NASA said it was "pretty comfortable" with how the Mars rovers were going and so was happy about repurposing the hardware or, as one speaker put it, "can we give it a new paint job?"

A source told The Register that morale at the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) was not high at present. Raiding successful programs to fulfill the administration's whims is unlikely to have improved the mood of engineers.
Still. Another trundlebot on the Moon. Far better than using that spare RTG for yet another deep space mission, right? ®

6b71eb9713c14243: In sports, a “dead rubber” is a match that takes place after the outcome of the series or championship has already been decided. But anyone who decided to skip this year’s Brazilian Grand Prix this past weekend missed one of the year’s most entertaining races, as a combination of a mixed-up starting order, some very fast drivers at the back, and a wet track that dried and then saw rain again resulted in action aplenty.

A peculiarity of F1 is that even if you manage to win a championship, there’s no guarantee you’ll be in a position to defend it. 950f1f8b6bbd8c4b: Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking.

Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on.

Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release.
The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1.

There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident, tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another.

Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog.

The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata.

The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported earlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel.

Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release.

Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest.
And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®
6c43d02e7e794ae5: Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the company scrambling to clean up a breach affecting shoppers in the UK, US, and Australia.

In an email sent to affected customers over the weekend, seen by The Register, the loo roll seller warns that personal information was accessed without authorization after a security incident at an unnamed US-based marketing software provider.

The email explains that the intruder gained access to the supplier's systems on October 30. The provider spotted the intrusion the following day and says it secured its systems by November 1, although Who Gives A Crap wasn't told until November 6. It's unclear why the supplier sat on the bad news for another five days before passing it on.

The exposed information includes customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, and total spending with the company. In other words, someone may now know not only where you live, but just how much of your hard-earned cash you've flushed down the crapper.

Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question.
"We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse.

In a separate public statement, Who Gives A Crap co-founder and CEO Simon Griffiths confirmed that the incident affected customers across the company's Australian, UK, and US stores. Canadian customers, meanwhile, appear to have escaped this particular toilet emergency, with the supplier reporting that no personal information belonging to shoppers in the country was accessed.

Who Gives A Crap says it has since disconnected the provider from its systems, changed access credentials, and begun warning affected customers to watch out for suspicious emails, texts, calls, and other unsolicited communications.
"The main concern is scam or phishing messages that use your real details to look convincing," the company warned in its customer email.

While Who Gives A Crap has been busy cleaning up, the supplier at the center of this particular stink remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified the software provider or disclosed how many customers were affected, including those in the UK, and didn’t respond to our questions.

Griffiths said the company is "engaging with the relevant regulatory authorities, as required." In the UK, the ICO told The Register: "We can confirm Who Gives A Crap Limited has reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided."
Who Gives A Crap has plenty of toilet paper to hand, although cleaning up this particular situation might require more than a few rolls. ®
72dbc45ba6d5009f: Good Monday morning. Last week, the UK imposed one of the strictest, most vague (and therefore overly broad) new laws around pornography in recent memory. Recording yourself having consensual kinky sex in private could come with jail time, as could watching other people do it. And sex workers are the ones to feel the repercussions of bad laws like these first, of course, with many reporting content disappearing from their online stores en masse. Keep reading to learn more about what it covers, and how creators are responding.
In the UK, Face Sitting Porn Might Land You in Jail

“I adore breath play. I love being strangled, suffocated and drowned, and I love strangling and suffocating others. Waterboarding: that’s my favourite,” Melissa Todd, a UK-based writer and sex worker, told me. “Many women do: it really isn’t only horrid men forcing us to do these dreadful depraved acts. Interrupting oxygen supply produces the most intense sensation of euphoria. I enjoy it in my private life, and I offer it in sessions too.”

Starting Friday, she and anyone else in the UK distributing or possessing certain types of choking, suffocation, breath play, strangulation and a bunch of other types of porn — even if it’s just recorded in the privacy of their homes and not for sale on a porn site — could face up to five years in prison.

This is, predictably, already a huge mess for sex workers. Adult creators watched platforms remove hundreds of their videos — even when the creators thought they were in compliance with the law. These creators say they were blindsided by the removals, since the content didn’t seem to violate the law at all. Creators are reporting one platform in particular, Clips4Sale, is purging content with little notice, “a precautionary measure,” with videos disappearing in the hundreds.

“Of course, we were all aware of the new Act coming in and prepared accordingly, but not for anything at this scale. We've had nothing since and they've been tweeting as normal,” adult creator Sophia Truee said. Clips4Sale launched in 2003 and caters heavily to fetish content. “It's a huge blow to this area of the industry, and I can only hope things will be communicated soon. We, as creators, understand how difficult it is to be a content site in this current climate, but communication has not been prioritized,” Truee said, noting that this is happening right before the holidays, with Black Friday being one of the most popular times for creators selling content. “For many, this will be devastating, as over 20 years of the work will have just been wiped.”

92c7545f4c38de01: The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices.

Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash.
"Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins.

"About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs."
Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare.

Its latest report, "An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register, have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use.

At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources of value.

A recent report from management consultants Bain & Company came to similar conclusions, estimating the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding all the infrastructure it needs, and this will require new uses beyond simply enhancing employee productivity.

Forrester also claims that the forces making AI abundant also make parts of the market unstable, and says that enterprise users should take heed of how prices collapsed as major providers like Anthropic slashed token costs in response to competition from open source models.

If demand disappoints as new capacity comes online, suppliers could cut investment, merge, change prices, or discontinue products. Customers could find themselves rebuilding AI plans around suppliers and services that no longer exist.
Forrester advises businesses to track whether their AI projects deliver measurable value and limit their exposure to vulnerable suppliers – with its help, of course.

Companies can judge how things are going by looking at the gap between suppliers' contracted business and revenue actually recognized, along with how they fund their build-outs. If a vendor leans more on outside investment and customer prepayments, as Oracle and CoreWeave have, this is a red flag to cut back dependencies on them, Forrester says.

Enterprises should also stress-test AI plans against scenarios such as a key vendor announcing end of support in 12 months, and an AI model supplier defaulting on payments to its compute vendor and cutting back service-level agreements for enterprise workloads. Companies should know in advance which AI use cases to drop, what data and workloads need to be moved, and at what cost.

But Hopkins sounded a further note of caution: "Oversupply on its own won't decide whether a correction comes. Demand will, and that's the biggest unknown, because it depends on enterprises finding lasting value in AI beyond simple productivity gains."

Organizations shouldn't pull back, he insists. They should keep investing where AI delivers value that can be demonstrated, closely monitor the financial health of the companies building AI computing, and be ready for corrections.
Recently, the International Monetary Fund started ringing alarm bells that financial markets are increasingly exposed to an AI-driven correction that could lead to widespread economic disruption.

Earlier this year, the Bank for International Settlements also raised concerns that the current situation with the AI industry bore the hallmarks of historical economic bubbles and presented a risk to global economic stability. ®

fb2a8a274448308b: Protesters on Nov. 5 burn a effigy depicting now ex-President Santiago Pena outside Congress in Asuncion, Paraguay, days after the beginning of a banking crisis to which he was linked. AP Photo/Jorge SaenzIt started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money. In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes. The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development. Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs. As scholars with expertise in various aspects of Paraguay’s contemporary political, economic and environment development, we believe the collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails. The political relationships through which financial institutions grow, regulators exercise authority and public resources are entrusted to private companies are crucial national concerns, especially in a country that has presented itself internationally as a model of economic stability. A bank that grew faster than scrutiny Founded as a digital lender in 2021, Ueno attracted customers with mobile banking and cash-back offers. Its expansion brought useful services to people underserved by conventional banks, including rural customers. Ueno also expanded the credit card market to low-income customers, an unprecedented move compared to previously restricted banking practices. As Ueno expanded, Paraguay increasingly attracted investors drawn by its low taxes, economic stability and business-friendly policies. Promoted by some as a “Dubai of South America,” the country also became a magnet for conservative influencers, particularly from Brazil, who contrasted Paraguay’s economic model with the purported mismanagement of left-wing governments elsewhere in the region. Indeed, under President Santiago Peña, Paraguay has been one of Latin America’s most enthusiastic allies of the Trump administration and its expansive regional vision. But beneath the financial stability, Ueno stood at the precipice of a much deeper problem. Congress President Basilio Núñez places the presidential sash on Pedro Alliana as he takes office as Paraguay’s new president on Nov. 6, 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz The central bank finally acted after accounting adjustments left Ueno’s solvency ratio below half the legal minimum. But problems had surfaced earlier. That included a supervisory report put out by the bank regulators in June 2026 that described roughly US$146 million in loans to three companies linked to Grupo Vázquez, Ueno’s controlling shareholder. Some companies had been transferred to group employees; supervisors questioned the collateral and ultimate use of the funds. That these warning signs went unheeded raises a related question of why regulators didn’t have a better handle on the situation and were not better able to contain the exposure. In any case, Ueno’s problems were exposed in dramatic fashion on Nov. 2, when the central bank placed Ueno into resolution, a process similar to bankruptcy but managed directly by Paraguay’s central bank. The lender, which says it has nearly 3 million customers – about half of the country’s population – halted transactions. The crisis quickly ensnared the governing party. Peña, an economist by training who was elected president in 2023 and had close ties to the bank, resigned on Nov. 5. The Senate then voted unanimously to remove him from office, thereby stripping Peña of his parliamentary immunity. He was swiftly put under house arrest, charged with corruption and succeeded by his Vice President Pedro Alliana, who was sworn in to serve until 2028. Meanwhile, the crisis has led to widespread protests, including outside Congress, with citizens accusing Peña and the ruling Colorado Party of “stealing” their savings. When the regulator knows the regulated Part of the story of Ueno is a tale of the closeness between political and financial elites in Paraguay. Carlos Carvallo chaired Ueno’s predecessor bank before Peña appointed him Paraguay’s central bank president in 2023. Carvallo resigned on Nov. 3 and has since been charged with the same corruption crimes as Peña. For its part, the Paraguayan central bank says Carvallo recused himself from any Ueno decisions. Yet the potential conflicts of interest ran much deeper. Peña previously directed Banco Basa, linked to Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, who retains considerable influence and was instrumental in helping push Peña out of office. Finance Minister Carlos Fernández Valdovinos also served on Basa’s board. Local reporters had documented these revolving-door relationships early in Peña’s term. Peña reportedly held a 1.58% stake in Ueno Holding, which shared its principal shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, with Ueno bank. His brother Francisco held shares in Luxembourg-based U Holdings, an indirect shareholder in the bank. Another shareholder was Juan Carlos López Moreira, Cartes’ former chief of staff. Both brothers exited in 2025. Peña has denied any wrongdoing, while prosecutors are examining allegations concerning his former business interests and his administration’s financial supervision. The inclusion of significant reserves of public funds made these connections especially consequential. Ueno held approximately $850 million in public funds, including $355 million from the country’s social security system, IPS, including health and retirement funds. It amounted to roughly 9% of IPS’s investment portfolio. Under Peña-appointed chairman Jorge Brítez, IPS relaxed eligibility requirements for bank deposits in 2023 and removed a capital-based exposure limit in 2024. Over the same period, its deposits at Ueno rose sharply. Grupo Vázquez’s technology firm ITTI won at least $2.3 million in state contracts after Peña took office, versus $675,000 before. ITTI attributed the increase to business expansion and denied a conflict of interest. Together these ties and regulatory changes raise important questions about regulatory capture and other potential conflicts of interest. What the growth figures leave out Paraguay’s economic gains are real. In August, the International Monetary Fund projected 4.4% growth in 2026 following 6.6% in 2025. Moody’s granted the country’s debt investment-grade status in 2024, and S&P followed in 2025. Hydroelectric power exports, agriculture and new infrastructure continue to underpin the economy. Demonstrators burn Ueno bank cards during a protest after Paraguay’s central bank took over the bank amid a solvency crisis on Nov. 5, 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz Washington is also drawing Paraguay more firmly into its regional economic strategy. On Oct. 23, the country became the 26th signatory to the Pax Silica Declaration, an initiative involving critical minerals, hydropower and advanced computing infrastructure. While the announcement did not specify financing commitments, it shows how Paraguay’s resources and perceived political predictability are being positioned as strategic assets. But growth figures and credit ratings say little about who shapes financial oversight or bears the costs of banking failures. Paraguay’s legacies of political patronage make it necessary to examine political and corporate connections and changes to public-fund investment rules. The social toll and the Colorado question Paraguay has been here before. Between 1995 and 1998, 13 banks and 35 financial firms closed, with direct costs estimated by the IMF at 10% to 13% of the country’s GDP. This preceded a smaller bank crisis in the early 2000s. Both ordeals exposed weak supervision and connected lending. Paraguay’s deposit guarantee, which covers balances up to about $38,000, is meant to limit depositor losses, and the Paraguayan Central Bank insists that failure is isolated in the latest case. Yet account transfers have already strained the system, producing outages at several banking institutions. Yet for most Paraguayans, the crisis was experienced not through technical financial or macroeconomic indicators but at the stark level of seeing from their phones that they couldn’t access their money. Wages, pensions and savings froze simultaneously. Young Ueno employees burned their company cards outside the Labor Ministry, demanding unpaid wages. Riot police used pepper spray and rubber bullets against depositors marching on Congress. For small businesses that banked and paid staff through Ueno, the real economy stopped. This widespread anger challenges the ruling party’s claims to the economic vision they cite as the engine for future growth. Whether it leads to institutional change or a reshuffle within the Colorado Party remains an open question. The test is how Paraguayan legislators and regulators will move forward and whether they separate banking supervision and public deposits from partisan and business networks. In any case, the myth of the “Dubai of South America” has come under serious scrutiny. While the protests were noteworthy, the Colorado Party has for now managed to resolve its own internal crisis by quickly sacrificing key political elites, including the president. Marco Castillo Ph.D., Paraguayan sociologist, recent graduate and former director of research at the Center for Latin American, Latino and Caribbean Studies at Graduate Center CUNY, and Sheyla Rios Galeano, a Ph.D. Student in human dimensions of natural resources, Colorado State University, contributed to this article. 91ae548d2cb1abf2: Advisers for COP30 President Andre Correa do Lago, center, talk after a Colombia delegate's request to speak was overlooked at the U.N. summit in 2025. Pablo Porciuncula/AFP via Getty ImagesNearly every country in the world has acknowledged that climate change is a serious problem. It’s hard to ignore, as billions of people suffer through increasingly destructive storms and extreme heat. In response, most governments have promised repeatedly to cut greenhouse gas emissions that are driving global temperatures higher. Yet those emissions are still hitting record levels, and global negotiations over how to slow climate change routinely end with weak promises. There’s a reason: All it takes to water down a deal during these negotiations – the 2026 U.N. climate conference started Nov. 9 – are a few voices obstructing progress, often without ever saying “no,” and all the while maintaining the appearance of being a climate leader. As a professor of environmental studies and international relations at the University of Southern California, I’ve attended and observed international climate negotiations for over a decade. My research lab investigates climate justice concerns and the forces that obstruct progress at the global U.N. climate talks. As world leaders and their negotiators meet for the latest climate talks, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9-20, you can also pick out who is obstructing progress. Here are five tactics among many that powerful people at these conferences use to delay, weaken or redirect meaningful action while still appearing committed to addressing climate change: 1. Say we can’t afford it “We don’t have the money” is a familiar refrain at U.N. climate negotiations. At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, wealthy countries pointed to tight budgets, pandemic debt and rising inflation as reasons they could not meet the US$1.3 trillion in assistance that developing countries were demanding. They instead offered $300 billion annually by 2035 as a finance target. Poorer countries that did little to cause climate change want longtime fossil fuel users to pay for the damage emissions have caused. The COP29 agreement itself estimated that developing countries’ climate needed $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion in total through 2030. In reality, affordability is really about priorities. For example, the International Institute for Sustainable Development found that governments around the world provided more than $1.2 trillion in public financial support for fossil fuels in 2024, about five times the $254 billion they provided for clean energy. Military budgets tell a similar story. Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the U.S. contributed $2 billion to the Green Climate Fund, meant to support poorer countries as they adapt to climate change, while Congress simultaneously approved at least $79 billion to help foreign countries by U.S. military weapons. Recent research points out that rising military spending makes climate goals even harder to reach because so much military activity runs on fossil fuels. The money exists. The question is where governments choose to spend it. 2. Promise to fix it later Another tactic is claiming that technological innovations will clean things up eventually, so drastic emissions cuts can wait or even be avoided. This technological optimism has deep roots. In 2004, Princeton scholars Steve Pacala and Robert Socolow proposed the “stabilization wedge” approach to addressing climate change. It slices future emissions growth into 15 strategy wedges, each representing a way to cut 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide. Selecting from that menu, government could piece together a suitable emissions reduction strategy. Carbon capture and storage allows fossil fuel operations to continue by pumping their emissions underground. Congressional Budget Office Renewable energy solutions such as solar and wind were proposed as wedges, but so were carbon capture and storage technologies – which would allow the burning of fossil fuels to continue. Scientists, including one of the original authors, have claimed that the wedges approach makes a difficult problem look deceptively simple to solve. Recent reporting by ProPublica tracked money behind the wedges project back to the fossil fuel giant BP. Yet the same logic is now present in agreements emerging from recent climate talks. 3. Water down the promise Another tactic is to agree to something, then water it down over time until it is no longer binding. At COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2022, early drafts of the agreement called for the “phasing out” of fossil fuels. It would have been a true milestone, as it was the first time the words “fossil fuels” had appeared in a climate agreement. However, after a late push led by India, backed by China, South Africa and others, the final text was changed to “phasedown” of “unabated” coal power instead. Additionally, the pact said nothing of oil and gas, the fuels that wealthier countries depend on most. U.S. Climate Envoy John Kerry and other delegates huddle for final negotiating at the closing sessions of COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2021. Kiara Worth/UNFCCC, CC BY-NC-SA The first fossil fuel language in a U.N. climate pact came out diluted. Four years later, at COP30, 88 countries backed a roadmap to move the world away from using fossil fuels, but the final decision left it out. 4. Make promises, then fail to deliver Countries are really good at making pledges to help, but not so much at providing the funding. In 2009, wealthy countries promised developing countries $100 billion annually to help them address climate risks. They missed that target for over a decade. Even when they did claim to hit the target, they relied largely on dubious accounting, with donors counting fossil fuel projects, airports and even ice cream shops as climate aid. The Loss and Damage Fund created at COP27 in 2021 to help countries manage disaster damage shows a similar pattern. Only about half of the roughly $822 million pledged had been paid in five years later, and the fund has not paid out a single dollar to a country hit by a disaster. Nepal has emerged as a critical test of the fund’s integrity. After a glacier collapse triggered a sudden flood that killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal in August 2026, the government estimated the country had suffered $2.7 billion in damage. Nepal requested $20 million, and, in a first, the fund’s board agreed in October to “provisionally set aside” $21.6 million, but that’s only the beginning of the paperwork. 5. Make decisions without everyone at the table Decisions at the U.N. climate conference are taken by consensus, meaning they’re considered adopted when no country formally objects. This act is marked by the banging of a gavel. At COP28 in Dubai, the conference president “gaveled through” a key decision before representatives of the Alliance of Small Island States had reached the room, meaning they had no chance to object. The lead negotiator for the islands’ group told the meeting that they would have objected, as they considered it too weak to keep warming to the agreed limit of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) within reach. In 2025, at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, a similar scene played out. After swiftly gaveling through many decisions, the conference president failed to recognize Colombia’s request to speak until after the gavel had fallen. Colombia objected that the text of the formal decision failed to discuss a transition away from fossil fuels. The COP president later apologized but said the decision could not be reopened. What to watch for at COP31 At COP31, my team and I will be watching for decisions about financial support, whether talk of technology crowds out reducing fossil fuel use, and who gets a voice. Much of what matters at these conferences happens out of the spotlight. Plenary sessions, where decisions are formally adopted, are the part most people see. But the wording of those decisions is usually worked out in smaller rooms and closed-door huddles among a handful of delegations. Small delegations can’t staff every room, and some rooms are closed to observers. My team will be tracking what happens, whose proposals survive, and what quietly drops out between drafts of the agreement text. We’ll also be paying attention to who, quietly or not, says “no.” Ridwan Intisaar Mahbub, a graduate student in public diplomacy, and Richie Sanchez, an undergraduate student in environmental studies at USC, contributed research for this article. ee0305ab71b3feaa: A woman in New Port Richey, Fla., voices her opposition to the construction of AI data centers on July 18, 2026. Thomas Simonetti/AFP via Getty ImagesData centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections. A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development. The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers. According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%. Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits. I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns. Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms. Data centers, like these near Social Circle, Ga., require enormous amounts of electricity. AP Photo/Mike Stewart Disrupting political polarization In contrast to many other issues, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines. Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points. The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally. Allies and adversaries Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care, given their methodological limitations. These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away. The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests. William Lawrence, a Democrat who flipped a red House seat in Michigan in the 2026 midterm elections, speaks on the campaign trail. AP Photo/Paul Sancya Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Similar concerns killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change. Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements. Politics as usual As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.” Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president. It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built. What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day. As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring. 4b382a44aa6e09e6: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails.
The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures.
Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information.

The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails.

The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required.

Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed.
Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's requirments, email began flowing once more.

SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both).
The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response.

To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place.
A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation."

"Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue."

Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected.
Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well.
It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®
Updated to add at 0922 UTC, November 10

Microsoft has confirmed that this was a fault. In its incident report (EX1545193), the company wrote: "A recent update to the spam enforcement rules caused email messages to be incorrectly marked and blocked, which led to impact."
It also said it would review its update procedures. This will be of great comfort to customers who found legitimate emails rejected by Microsoft's servers as a result of the latest whoopsie.

Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests

Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction.
The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree.

05bd9f0351a0c3a2: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance.

Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.”

Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust.

“Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers.

These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands.

Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.”

ab138347ee884e3e: NEW YORK, Nov 9 — Chips made by US chip titan Nvidia push the boundaries of artificial intelligence, but its leader Jensen Huang is in the spotlight over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Unknown to the public just four years ago, the 63-year-old is a powerful entrepreneur, drawing stadium crowds as he presents cutting-edge components essential to the development of AI tools like ChatGPT.
Media reports last week said US intelligence officials believe Huang grew close to a Chinese executive who was funnelling information to Beijing.
Nvidia’s board said yesterday it had opened a probe into the CEO and co-founder, who acknowledged having been unfaithful to his wife and said he was “deeply sorry.”

Big tech’s insatiable appetite for chips designed by Nvidia, known as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), has catapulted the California chipmaker to a market valuation of US$4.5 trillion (RM18.2 trillion), among the world’s largest.

Its meteoric rise has made Huang one of the world’s richest people — worth around US$160 billion, according to Forbes — thanks to the roughly four per cent stake he holds in the company he founded three decades ago with two friends in a Silicon Valley diner.
He has become a close informal adviser on AI to Donald Trump, travelling with the US president on Air Force One on a trip to Beijing earlier this year.
That is an area of concern to US officials who believe he has been involved with the alleged spy, Alice Huang, who is linked to a Singapore-based data centre company, according to the New York Times.
Despite their shared surname, the pair are not related.
Early life
Born in Taipei in 1963, Jensen Huang — originally named Jen-Hsun — embodies the American success story.
At nine years old, he was sent away with his brother to boarding school in small-town Kentucky.
His uncle recommended the school to his Taiwanese parents believing it to be a prestigious institution, though it was actually a school for troubled youth.

Too young to be a student, Huang boarded there but attended a nearby public school alongside the children of tobacco farmers. With his poor English, he was bullied and forced to clean toilets — a two-year ordeal that transformed him.
“We worked really hard, we studied really hard, and the kids were really tough,” he recounted in an interview with US broadcaster NPR.
But “the ending of the story is I loved the time I was there,” Huang said.
Brought home by his parents who had by then settled in the north-western US state of Oregon, he graduated from university at just 20 and joined AMD, then LSI Logic, to design chips — his passion.

But he wanted to go further and founded Nvidia in 1993 to “solve problems that normal computers can’t,” using semiconductors powerful enough to handle 3D graphics, he said during an interview on the “No Priors” podcast.

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang waves after a welcome ceremony for US President Donald Trump at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing May 14, 2026. Huang has rejected calls to deliberately slow down AI development even as some insiders warn the technology could threaten human existence within a decade. — AFP pic
‘As fast as we can’
Nvidia created the first GPU in 1999, riding the intersection of video games, data centres, cloud computing and now generative AI.
Always dressed in a black T-shirt and leather jacket, Huang sports a Nvidia logo tattoo and has a taste for sports cars.
One former high-ranking Nvidia employee described him to AFP as “the most driven person” he’d ever met.
He has rejected calls to deliberately slow down AI development even as some insiders warn the technology could threaten human existence within a decade.
“That kind of narrative is dramatic, it gets a lot of attention,” but “it’s not grounded on facts,” he told CBS News in September.
“We should go as fast as we can” on AI, but labs should not release products that are not safe, he said.
Street food
On visits to his native Taiwan, Huang is treated like a megastar, with fans crowding him for autographs and selfies as journalists follow him to the barber shop and his favourite night market.
“He has created the phenomena because of his personal charm,” noted Wayne Lin of Witology Market Trend Research Institute.

“A person like him must be very busy and his schedule should be full every day meeting big bosses. But he remembers to eat street food when he comes to Taiwan,” he said, calling Huang “unusually friendly.”

111b66d97ab01eca: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies.

In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed, the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030.

Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles.

But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational?

Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress.

The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year.

Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study.

The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes.

In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe, which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products.

But few other alternative-protein companies had such a deeply integrated way of using AI in product development, the AI-assisted review suggests. Meanwhile, the sector seems to be facing more fundamental problems, including stubbornly slow mainstream consumer adoption and declining funding levels. Most notably, venture capital flowing into cultivated meat fell from a $989 million peak in 2021 to around $83 million last year.

The transportation sector offers some hopeful examples of the type of AI integration necessary to achieve the study’s projections, particularly among battery manufacturers and ride-sharing platforms. CATL—which controls roughly 40% of the global market for electric-vehicle batteries—launched an AI system trained on more than 100,000 battery design cases and 600 terabytes of test data. It cut the time needed to screen candidate materials by two orders of magnitude, according to the company. Independent researchers also found that the ride-sharing platform Didi Chuxing was able cut per-trip emissions 16% on average by using AI-optimized routing to minimize detours.

There’s another big problem in the climate case for AI, though: Oil and gas companies are also interested in these tools for many reasons, including the potential to increase production of fossil fuels. Technology firms that committed to sustainability goals in the past should answer questions about how their tools could be used to boost old, dirty energy as well as clean, renewable energy.

Finally, it’s also worth noting that integrating AI is just the first step, and it remains unclear to what degree the technology can accelerate the sorts of improvements and innovations envisioned. AI also does little to shorten the standard paths to certifying, permitting, building, packaging, marketing, and selling any resulting products, facilities, or services.

The findings of the analysis, carried out by Anthropic’s Claude Code, were reviewed against public documents and media accounts to ensure their accuracy. It is possible that some companies and utilities in these industries are pursuing AI-assisted applications that would fit into the initial study’s scenarios but haven’t yet been disclosed publicly.

Greater and better-targeted AI integration and efficiency gains in these three sectors may well materialize, bringing the 2035 projections closer to reality. But it won’t happen without deliberate and sustained efforts to ensure that AI delivers more environmental benefits than harms.

Notably, so far the rapid adoption of AI models and buildout of data centers has driven a huge increase in energy consumption and emissions, and this has led major tech companies like Microsoft, Google, and others to fall well off track in their corporate climate goals. At this point it would be surprising if the sector even manages to zero out its climate pollution: Emissions associated with global data centers (which may handle AI as well as non-AI computing tasks) could exceed 300 million tons annually in 2035, according to the IEA’s base forecast.

Industry leaders must implement the technology in the ways that promise to do the most to drive down emissions. Corporate customers should select models with the lowest environmental impacts and opt to work with the AI developers doing the most to reduce their climate footprint. And states and regions need to do more to incentivize or require all these companies to operate in more responsible ways.
The need has never been more apparent.
Mary Nichols is distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board.
Jeremy Tamanini is the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm.

c35a133ff9697d5c: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
Originally published on Global Voices
Illustration by Nshua Cali-Dibang. Used with permission.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Every search, social media interaction, and conversation with an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can leave behind information about its user. Individually, these digital traces may appear insignificant. Collectively, however, they can reveal interests, habits, preferences and patterns of behavior that have considerable commercial and political value.

As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, technology companies are finding new ways to use data to develop their products, personalize services and generate revenue. While these developments offer considerable benefits, they also raise a difficult question: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?

The issue extends beyond privacy policies and user agreements. It concerns the growing power of technology companies to collect information, draw conclusions about individuals, and influence the digital environments in which people communicate, work, and access information.
The business of knowing more about us

In September 2024, the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) published findings from an investigation into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch.

The FTC reported that these companies collected extensive information about users and, in some cases, non-users. The information included personal details, interests, online activities, and data obtained from other sources. The investigation also raised concerns about lengthy data retention, inadequate privacy protections, and the use of personal information in automated systems, including AI.

The report highlighted a fundamental imbalance: Companies can accumulate substantial information about individuals, while those individuals may have limited understanding of how their data is used or how to prevent certain uses.

AI adds another dimension to this problem. Data can help train models, improve recommendations, and power automated decisions. However, the greater the volume and variety of information companies can access, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on its collection and use.

The concern is not that every company collecting data is necessarily acting maliciously. Rather, it is that systems designed to maximize commercial value from information can create incentives to collect more data than people reasonably expect or understand.
Inclusion at what cost?

For millions of people, AI offers opportunities that were previously difficult to access. Students can use AI tools to support learning, small businesses can improve their operations, and journalists can explore new approaches to research and production.

In countries such as Nigeria, where access to resources and professional services can be uneven, these tools could help narrow certain gaps. AI systems that support local languages and reflect diverse cultural experiences could also make digital services more accessible.

Yet inclusion should mean more than allowing people to use a technology. It should also mean ensuring that they understand the conditions under which they use it and retain meaningful rights over their information.

Many digital services are governed by lengthy terms and privacy policies that users may accept without fully understanding the implications. Some AI products also raise questions about whether information submitted through prompts, uploaded documents, or other interactions may be retained or used to improve models.

The precise practices differ between companies and products. Nevertheless, users need clear explanations of what information is collected, why it is needed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for purposes beyond the immediate service.
Without these safeguards, the benefits of AI inclusion risk coming with an invisible cost: reduced control over personal information.
When corporate power begins to resemble surveillance

The connection between big tech and authoritarianism requires careful examination. Authoritarianism is not simply the collection of data by private companies. It involves the concentration and exercise of power in ways that undermine accountability, rights, and freedoms.

However, extensive corporate data collection can create conditions that make surveillance easier. Detailed personal information can support profiling, targeted persuasion and the prediction of individual behavior. Depending on the circumstances, businesses, governments, or other actors may exploit these capabilities.

The risks become particularly serious when personal data can be accessed or shared without adequate safeguards, when automated systems make consequential decisions without meaningful oversight, or when people have little opportunity to challenge how their information is used.

Concentrated corporate power adds another concern. When a small number of companies control widely used digital platforms, AI services, and large pools of information, individuals may have few practical alternatives. Leaving a platform may mean losing access to professional networks, customers, communities, or essential services.

This does not mean that every AI system is a surveillance tool or that every technology company intends to restrict freedom. It means that the infrastructure of digital life deserves scrutiny because its capabilities can be used in ways that extend beyond their original commercial purpose.
Nigeria’s data protection challenge

Nigeria has a legal framework intended to protect individuals against the misuse of their personal information. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and provides a framework for the lawful, fair and accountable processing of personal data.
Legislation is an important step, but effective protection also depends on implementation, public awareness, and regulators’ ability to hold organizations accountable.

As Nigerians increasingly adopt AI-powered services, questions about data governance become more pressing. Users need to understand their rights, while organizations must take responsibility for explaining their practices and protecting the information they collect.

There is also a wider question of representation. If AI systems are developed using data that inadequately reflects Nigerian languages, cultures, and social realities, their benefits may be distributed unevenly. Responsible AI governance must therefore address both the protection of personal information and the inclusion of communities whose experiences are often underrepresented.

UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence emphasizes privacy, data protection, transparency, accountability, and fairness throughout the AI lifecycle. These principles provide a useful foundation for ensuring that technological progress respects human rights.
Innovation must not come at the expense of control

The challenge is not to reject AI or prevent companies from using data to develop useful technologies. It is to establish boundaries that allow innovation without making personal privacy an acceptable casualty.

Technology companies should minimize unnecessary data collection, communicate their policies clearly, provide meaningful choices, and strengthen protections against unauthorized access. Regulators must ensure that existing laws remain effective as AI capabilities evolve, while users need accessible information about the rights available to them.

Ultimately, digital inclusion cannot be measured solely by the number of people using AI. It must also consider whether those people can participate safely, understand the systems they rely on, and exercise meaningful control over their information.

As AI becomes more powerful, the question is no longer simply what technology can do with our data. It is who decides what can be done, who benefits from those decisions, and who has the power to challenge them.
The future of AI should not be defined only by what machines learn about us, but also by how much control we retain over ourselves.
Written by Nshua Cali-Dibang
